item.title: Sanofi agrees to buy lung-disease drugmaker Insmed for about $41 billion in cash
item.description: Sanofi will pay $175 a share in cash for US drugmaker Insmed, a 46% premium, to add the fast-selling lung drug Brinsupri and reduce its reliance on Dupixent. (BioXconomy, Quartz)

item.title: New York Fed's Williams says inflation is too high and does not rule out rate increases at consecutive meetings
item.description: John Williams said restoring 2% inflation is "100 percent essential", expects inflation of about 3.5% this year, and told reporters that raising rates at back-to-back meetings remains possible. (Federal Reserve Bank of New York, The Jakarta Post (Reuters))

item.title: EU caps hybrid car imports from 1 December, limiting China to about 191,780 vehicles over 200 days
item.description: The European Commission has published temporary quotas on hybrid car imports from China, Japan, Turkey, South Korea, the UK and others, aimed mainly at a surge of Chinese hybrids. (The Guardian, electrive)

item.title: Best Buy raises its annual forecast after comparable sales grow 6.1%, its best quarter in five years
item.description: The electronics retailer beat its own expectations on computing, phones and new categories such as AI glasses, and lifted full-year sales and profit guidance ahead of the holidays. (Best Buy (Business Wire release), Rallies)

item.title: Five Facts About Stablecoins
item.description: Wallet-level blockchain data from 2020 to 2025 suggest dollar stablecoins are now used as money for payments rather than mainly for crypto speculation, with little sign that they drain bank deposits. (Lin William Cong, Gordon Y. Liao, Eswar S. Prasad et al. · Nanyang Technological University; Circle; Cornell University; Arizona State University)

item.title: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about $43.9 billion
item.description: CrowdStrike will pay 1.135 of its shares for each Zscaler share, a 34% premium, to add network security to its device-security platform; its own shares fell more than 8% premarket. (Zscaler (joint press release), The Globe and Mail)

item.title: Taiwan eases margin-call rules as Asian authorities try to halt an AI-driven stock rout
item.description: After the Taiex lost 17.5% in a week, Taiwan cut the margin-maintenance threshold to 120% from 130%, tightened short-selling rules and kept its stabilization fund in the market; the index rebounded 2.16% on Monday. (Focus Taiwan (CNA), Focus Taiwan (CNA), The Globe and Mail (Reuters))

item.title: Trump threatens a "tremendous tax" on US companies that build AI data centres abroad
item.description: President Trump said US firms that build data centres overseas would face a heavy tax, but gave no details and said his staff were hearing the idea for the first time. (BBC, The Globe and Mail (AP))

item.title: A Missouri judge approves Bayer's $7.25 billion settlement of Roundup cancer claims
item.description: A St Louis state court found the deal "fair, reasonable and adequate", potentially ending most of the litigation that has weighed on Bayer since it bought Monsanto in 2018. (The Guardian, Insurance Journal)

item.title: Past Automation and Future AI: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion
item.description: Jones and Tonetti find that automation explains essentially all US productivity growth since 1950, and that AI should speed growth up, but slowly, because tasks still done by people hold the economy back. (Charles I. Jones, Christopher Tonetti · Stanford GSB, Anthropic, NBER)

item.title: An AI sell-off pushes the S&P 500 and the Dow into a correction as Nvidia falls about 14%
item.description: The S&P 500 fell 3.7% and the Nasdaq 5.28% on Friday, pushing the S&P 500 and Dow into a correction and erasing the Nasdaq's gains for the year as AI stocks slumped. (Fox Business, Yahoo Finance, Quartz)

item.title: The UK and EU agree deals on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility, but tuition fees remain unresolved
item.description: The UK and EU agreed to ease Brexit checks on food, relink their emissions trading schemes and create a youth mobility scheme, in exchange for UK alignment with EU rules in those areas. (The Guardian, BBC)

item.title: Intuit agrees to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, less than a third of what it paid
item.description: Intuit will sell email marketing platform Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, less than a third of the roughly $12 billion it paid in 2021, and use the cash to buy back shares. (Intuit, TechCrunch)

item.title: Canadian retail sales rise 0.8% in September on higher gas prices, but an early estimate points to a 1.5% drop in October
item.description: Canadian retail sales rose 0.8% to $75.3 billion in September, mostly on higher prices at gas stations, while sales volumes rose just 0.1% and an early estimate shows a 1.5% fall in October. (Statistics Canada, The Globe and Mail)

item.title: Gambling for Goals
item.description: Using a survey linked to millions of Korean credit, telecom and card records, economists find that people who see life goals like homeownership as out of reach take more financial risks, such as trading crypto. (Costas Arkolakis, Spencer Y. Kwon, Dominic Russel et al.)

item.title: US retail sales rise just 0.2% in October as car purchases fall and prices outpace spending
item.description: US retail and food-service sales rose 0.2% in October to $748.2 billion, slowing from 0.8% in September, as auto dealers' sales fell and consumer prices rose faster than spending. (U.S. Census Bureau, StockAnalysis, The Globe and Mail)

item.title: Walmart raises its annual outlook for the third time as US online sales grow 23%
item.description: Walmart's quarterly sales rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion and it raised its full-year guidance again, as shoppers across income groups seek lower prices and its online, marketplace and advertising businesses grow fast. (Walmart, The Globe and Mail)

item.title: Japan's core inflation rises to 2.2% in October, its fastest this year, as energy subsidies end
item.description: Japan's core consumer prices rose 2.2% from a year earlier in October, up from 2.1%, as expiring energy subsidies lifted power and gas bills, keeping a December Bank of Japan rate hike in view. (Xinhua, MLQ.ai, ActionForex)

item.title: Canada seeks an interim tariff deal with the US by year-end, but says some sector tariffs will stay
item.description: Ottawa wants an interim deal by year-end to lower US tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, but its trade minister says some tariffs will remain. (CBC News via Yahoo News Canada, Reuters via Free Malaysia Today)

item.title: The Labor Market Impact of Temporary High-Skill Immigration Programs
item.description: Temporary high-skill visa programs such as H-1B cut earnings of native science and engineering graduates by about 3.3%, but raised average US wages by about 1.3%, Borjas estimates. (George J. Borjas · Harvard Kennedy School)

item.title: Fed minutes show almost all officials expect further rate hikes, and a couple raised the idea of a half-point move
item.description: Minutes of the Fed's October 27-28 meeting show officials held rates at 3.75-4% but almost all expect more hikes, setting up a December debate over how fast to tighten. (Federal Reserve, Federal Reserve (minutes), The Globe and Mail)

item.title: Lowe's raises its full-year sales forecast to about $92.5 billion as online sales jump 17.4%
item.description: Lowe's comparable sales rose 1.8% last quarter and it now expects full-year sales of about $92.5 billion, though it trimmed its margin forecast as costs rise. (Lowe's, Hardware Retailing)

item.title: Palo Alto Networks raises its revenue forecast after 39% growth and agrees to buy Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock
item.description: The cybersecurity company now expects fiscal 2027 revenue of up to $14.57 billion and is buying an AI model-training startup founded only last year. (Proactive Investors, MLQ.ai)

item.title: Alibaba's cloud revenue grows 53% as AI demand accelerates, but heavy spending keeps free cash flow negative
item.description: Alibaba's group revenue rose 10% to about $40.5 billion, its AI cloud unit grew 53%, and free cash flow was an outflow of $5.1 billion as data-centre spending climbed. (Alibaba Group (Business Wire via Yahoo Finance), Grafa, Crypto Briefing)

item.title: Irregular Demand: The Anti-Compromise Effect in the Field
item.description: In a Lyft experiment with 7.2 million riders, adding an expensive premium ride pushed customers toward the cheapest option and toward not riding at all. (Nicola Gennaioli, John A. List, Matthias Rodemeier et al. · Bocconi University; University of Chicago; Australian National University; Washington University in St. Louis)

item.title: Nvidia's quarterly revenue doubles to $115.8 billion, and the board says it will not bring Jensen Huang back
item.description: Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago, guided to about $130 billion next quarter, and its chair said the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang. (Nvidia, BBC, TechCrunch)

item.title: ECB warns that AI valuations and debt-funded data centres leave markets exposed to an abrupt correction
item.description: The ECB's November Financial Stability Review says risks remain elevated, led by stretched AI valuations, rising government borrowing and geoeconomic tensions, though euro area banks look resilient. (European Central Bank)

item.title: UK inflation rises to 3.6%, a one-year high, as diesel reaches a record price
item.description: UK consumer prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5%, driven by motor fuel, while core inflation held near 2.8% and energy bills are forecast to jump in January. (Office for National Statistics, BBC)

item.title: Target raises its sales forecast after a third strong quarter, with comparable sales up 5.6%
item.description: Target's third-quarter net sales rose 7.1% to $27.1 billion, comparable sales grew 5.6% against estimates of 3.5%, and it now expects full-year sales growth of about 6%. (Target, The Globe and Mail)

item.title: Canadian Natural Resources agrees to buy Advantage Energy for $2.53 billion to expand in Alberta's Montney
item.description: Canadian Natural Resources will pay $13.55 in cash per Advantage Energy share, a deal worth about $2.53 billion including debt, adding roughly 79,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day near Grande Prairie. (Canadian Natural Resources (news release via BOE Report), The Globe and Mail, BNN Bloomberg)

item.title: Monetary policy in a Phelps–Winter Economy
item.description: Greenwald and Stiglitz argue that in markets where firms hold on to captive customers, higher interest rates push firms to raise prices, weakening rate hikes as a tool against inflation. (Bruce C. Greenwald, Joseph E. Stiglitz · Columbia University)

item.title: Canadian inflation holds at 3.1% in October as gasoline keeps the headline rate above target while core measures stay near 2%
item.description: Canada's consumer prices rose 3.1% over the year to October, unchanged from September and just under forecasts, with gasoline up 30.9% but inflation excluding energy easing to 2.0%. (Statistics Canada, The Globe and Mail)

item.title: Tiff Macklem will leave the Bank of Canada when his term ends in June 2027, and the board starts the search for a successor
item.description: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem will not seek a second term when his seven-year term expires on June 2, 2027; the board aims to pick a successor by spring. (Bank of Canada, BNN Bloomberg (The Canadian Press))

item.title: Quebecor makes a $31-billion cash-and-stock proposal to buy Telus, which would cut Canada's national wireless carriers from four to three
item.description: Quebecor proposed buying larger rival Telus for about C$19.45 a share, a 60% premium, in a non-binding offer that Telus's board says carries significant regulatory and governance risks. (Quebecor (Cision newswire), The Globe and Mail, The Globe and Mail (Business Brief))

item.title: Canada and China widen their tariff arrangement as Carney meets Xi, with relief for pork and seafood and a revived currency swap
item.description: China will cut tariffs on about C$400 million of Canadian pork and seafood exports, and Canada will extend and widen tariff refunds on Chinese steel and aluminium it cannot source at home. (The Globe and Mail, Reuters (via TimesLIVE), BNN Bloomberg (The Canadian Press))

item.title: Home Depot names finance chief Richard McPhail as CEO and reports quarterly sales of $43.4 billion, ahead of estimates
item.description: Home Depot promoted CFO Richard McPhail to chief executive from November 23 and posted third-quarter sales of $43.4 billion, while do-it-yourself spending stays weak. (The Home Depot (PR Newswire), The Globe and Mail)

item.title: How Does Capital Flow To Poor Countries? Evidence from Venture Capital and Private Equity
item.description: A survey experiment with 1,485 venture capital and private equity investors in 108 countries finds that identical firms attract much less interest when located in poorer countries, especially from non-specialist investors. (Emanuele Colonnelli, Marcio Cruz, Josh Lerner et al.)

item.title: Japan's economy shrinks at a 0.1% annualized rate in the third quarter, its first contraction in four quarters
item.description: Japan's real GDP edged down 0.02% in July-September, a 0.1% annualized fall that missed forecasts of growth, as households cut spending while business investment rose 1.6%. (Cabinet Office of Japan, Xinhua)

item.title: China's October retail sales grow just 0.4% and investment falls 8.1%, missing forecasts across the board
item.description: China's retail sales, factory output and fixed-asset investment all came in below expectations in October, with consumer spending nearly flat and property investment down 21.6% so far this year. (National Bureau of Statistics of China, ING Think, Quartz)

item.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail to protect its auto industry
item.description: Days before meeting Xi Jinping, Mark Carney said Canada will pursue European, Chinese or Japanese carmakers if a US deal does not leave it a viable auto sector. (The Guardian, Euronews, The Globe and Mail)
